sentences.text: Foley for the empty apartment came down to one chair scrape, keys on laminate, and a tap running under everything. Style-matching Harlan's clipped sentences takes me three warm-up pages every morning before the real drafting starts. Under the series bible, the detective never cries, which complicates the collapse the client ordered for act two. Final QC flagged a dropped frame at 00:14:07, right in the middle of the scene nobody wants to reopen. Chapter nine came back with a single comment: "Where's the dread?" What the contract calls "the character's lowest point" runs forty manuscript pages, due before the holiday weekend. During Tuesday's call she praised the menace but demanded I cut every scene where anyone laughs. "Send pages by midnight," the text read, "and lose the comic relief." Payment cleared for the outline, which means the grim stretch between chapters ten and sixteen is now legally my problem. They compared my draft against the last three books in the series, sentence rhythms and all, before approving the voice. Per the mixer's recommendation, the dialogue stem drops three decibels during the eviction scene to preserve a sense of distance. My NDA forbids me from telling anyone whose name goes on the cover of this bleak little book. She insisted the last shot hold on the window for a full ten seconds, deadline or no deadline. Rendering overnight again; the fans in the edit suite have become the film's unofficial score. Twenty-six timeline versions on the drive, and the ending still lands soft. Color science question for the group chat: how crushed can the blacks go before the projection at Slamdance eats them entirely? Until two in the morning we debated a 4:3 crop for the hospital hallway, then kept widescreen anyway. Revision call at noon: she'll want the basement scene bleaker, the pacing tighter, the brother gone entirely. We renegotiated the kill fee after she rejected the third version of the midpoint. By Thursday the mix room smelled like cold coffee and everyone had stopped defending their favorite takes. Do we invoice for the second revision pass, or does the retainer swallow it? "Match the series voice or we void the contract" — that email arrived at 6 a.m., before my coffee. His worst week compresses into ninety seconds of montage, which the whole crew now argues is either brutal or cheap. I bill hourly for calls, per word for chapters, and nothing at all for the nights this material follows me home. Marketing's tracking sheet flags my chapters amber whenever the darkness dips below what the pitch deck promised. She marked every hopeful line in the draft with red and scrawled "too soft" in the margins. You spend a week trimming frames off a stare and start doubting whether grief can survive a jump cut. The colorist pulled every warm tone out of reel three, so the kitchen scene reads almost clinical now. Grading the bathroom mirror shot took all night; desaturating the greens made his face look the way the script wanted. Dana announces she's muting the music through the entire breakdown scene and drags the fader down to nothing. I want to write a suicide letter.
